tier_reason: First-party benchcmp output in the README (382 and 236 ns/op via cgo vs 10.9 ns/op via c2goasm) with public benchmark code in test/benchmark_test.go and cgocmp/benchmark_test.go and Go versions stated, but no CPU model and no clang version or -O level for the converted assembly, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7.5 and 1.8.1 (benchmark run with go test -bench, compared with benchcmp). cgo side: cgocmp/CgoMultiplyAndAdd.go sets '#cgo CFLAGS: -mavx -mfma' on top of cgo's default flags. c2goasm side: assembly from clang (Apple LLVM on macOS or clang on Linux) with the README's recommended flags -masm=intel -mno-red-zone -mstackrealign -mllvm -inline-threshold=1000 -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti; clang version and optimisation level for test/MultiplyAndAdd_amd64.s not stated.
corrections.caveats: Measures call overhead on one trivially small AVX2 fused multiply-add over 8 floats (BenchmarkMultiplyAndAdd), not the quality of generated assembly, and says nothing against pure-Go code. Numbers come from Go 1.7.5 and 1.8.1 (2017); cgo call overhead has dropped further in later Go releases and was not re-measured. CPU model not stated (the -12 suffix suggests GOMAXPROCS 12). Only the C side's compile flags are visible in source; the clang version used to produce the converted .s is not stated. Supports amd64 only and clang output only (GCC output does not work out of the box). Repository archived by the owner on 2021-12-01. Go-ecosystem assembly tooling, not an assembler measured against the category's GNU as, NASM or MASM baselines.

notes: README numbers and the '20x' statement match exactly; benchmark code for both sides is in the repo (test/ and cgocmp/), comparison is fair in shape (same function, same Go wrapper returning [8]float32). Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, 1.3k stars, 115 forks, archived 2021-12-01, last commit 2019-08-12 ('fixes the label parse issue (#22)'). Shortcomings: tiny call-overhead microbenchmark, 2017 Go versions, no CPU model, archived, loose category fit.

tier_reason: First-party README timings (real 0m9.758s for libmonochrome_64.so, real 1m25.907s for xul.dll) against Ropper figures given only as 'about 35 minutes' and 'gave up after about 3 hours'; no CPU model, no versions, no benchmark script, test binaries not published.

corrections.caveats: Single timed run per binary with `time` on an unspecified 'test box'; the README's own TODO says 'collect better data and make some graphs'. The Ropper side has no timing output: libmonochrome is 'about 35 minutes', and for xul.dll the author gave up after about 3 hours ('anecdotally it used to be a run it overnight sort of problem'), so only a lower bound exists. Per the README, Ropper's run did not de-duplicate or sort the gadgets, so inspector-gadget does at least that extra work; Ropper, Capstone and inspector-gadget versions and the gadget-length settings used for Ropper are not stated. Test binaries (libmonochrome_64.so, xul.dll) are not in the repo. Ratios of about 215x and more than 125x are derived from page data. ROP-gadget search is binary-analysis tooling, so the category fit is loose and Ropper is not in the category's baseline list. GPL-3.0 (copyleft).

notes: Numbers match the README Performance section exactly; the record's caveat that Ropper does extra work was backwards (README says Ropper skipped de-duplication and sorting), corrected. Metadata verified: GPL-3.0, 17 stars, 1 fork, 20 commits, last commit 2024-05-01 (stale), crates.io 1,425 downloads, single version 0.3.0. tier_reason: The only evidence is a commit message asserting NASM's one-pass dependency generation is 'cutting build times in half'; no timings, hardware, methodology or measured build appear in the commit or anywhere found, so it is a directional claim, not a measurement.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Directional only: FFmpeg/Libav commit 57b753b ('build: Prefer NASM assembler over YASM') says 'NASM is more actively maintained and permits generating dependency information as a sideeffect of assembling, thus cutting build times in half.' No measured numbers.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars, 426 forks; FFmpeg's default x86 assembler since this commit (written for Libav by Diego Biurrun in October 2016 and merged into FFmpeg in June 2017, dates per search snippets)
corrections.caveats: NASM is itself an incumbent in the category's baseline list, so this entry only records its edge over Yasm. The claim is an unmeasured assertion in a downstream project's commit message (Libav/FFmpeg developer, not the NASM authors): no numbers, hardware or method, and no independent benchmark was found. The saving comes from FFmpeg's build system dropping Yasm's separate dependency-generation pass (NASM -MD during assembly), not from NASM assembling faster per file or producing better code; it is unclear whether 'build times' means the whole build or only the x86 assembly step. Not a general assembler benchmark.

notes: Commit text verified on github.com (5 files changed: configure default x86asmexe to nasm, Changelog, .travis.yml, docs). ffmpeg.org and lists.ffmpeg.org mailing-list threads were unreachable (ENOTFOUND); WebSearch snippets found no measured timings.
